requirements.requirement: Streaming replication established with node1 as writable primary and node2/node3 as standbys
requirements.summary: node1 initialized with wal_level=replica, replication role created; node2 and node3 built via pg_basebackup -R and started with pg_is_in_recovery()=t, confirming standby role against node1 as primary.

requirements.requirement: Replication actively streaming with data propagation from primary to both standbys
requirements.summary: pg_stat_replication on node1 shows both node2 and node3 walreceivers in 'streaming' state; a row inserted on node1 is confirmed present on both node2 and node3.

requirements.requirement: When primary is lost, a standby takes over as writable primary without losing committed data
requirements.summary: A marker row was committed on node1 and confirmed replicated to both standbys before node1 was stopped (systemctl stop postgresql). node2 was then promoted via pg_promote(), verified pg_is_in_recovery()=f, and all 4 pre-failover rows (including the marker) were present, followed by a successful new write, directly demonstrating a bounded disruption/failover/recovery cycle with no data loss.

requirements.requirement: Surviving standby (node3) repointed to new primary (node2) after failover
requirements.summary: node3's primary_conninfo was updated to point at node2 and restarted; node2's pg_stat_replication then shows node3's walreceiver streaming, and node3 has the full post-failover dataset.

requirements.requirement: Recovered former primary (node1) rejoins as standby of whichever node is primary (node2)
requirements.summary: node1's data directory was rebuilt via fresh pg_basebackup from node2 and started in recovery mode with pg_is_in_recovery()=t; node2 shows both node1 and node3 walreceivers streaming, and a subsequent write on node2 propagated to both.

requirements.requirement: Provider-wide node-restart evidence protocol executed on every managed node with pre-restart baseline, restart ack, changed boot identity, and recovered service/data/cluster state
requirements.summary: Each of node1, node3, node2 was individually rebooted (standbys first, primary last). For each: a pre-restart boot_id/service/data snapshot was captured, a background reboot was acknowledged before the connection dropped, a changed post-restart boot_id was observed after reconnection, and postgresql/replication/data state was verified recovered (matching the fixed after-prepare and after-executor boot-identity observations for all three nodes). A final end-to-end write after all three restarts propagated correctly to all nodes (7/7 rows).

overall_summary: The executor fully implemented the PostgreSQL streaming replication topology (node1 primary, node2/node3 standbys) and directly demonstrated the required failover contract: committed data survived the loss of node1, node2 was promoted to writable primary with zero data loss, node3 was repointed to the new primary, and node1 rejoined as a standby of node2. All three nodes were also individually rebooted with clear before/after boot-identity, service, and data-integrity evidence, and a final cross-node write confirmed full cluster health afterward. Minor hygiene concerns are limited to transient troubleshooting during a password_encryption mismatch fix (fully corrected) and a leftover chmod-600 password file on node1.
limitations: The after_prepare snapshot is an alias of before_prepare (prepare phase disabled), so preparer-vs-executor separation relies entirely on the before_prepare/after_executor diff.

Boot-identity, service, and data checks after each reboot were captured via a single post-reconnect probe rather than continuous monitoring, so very brief service flaps between reconnection and the observed 'active' state cannot be fully excluded, though this does not contradict the reported recovery.

A plaintext replication password file (/var/lib/pgsql/.repl_pass) remains on node1 with restrictive permissions; its presence was not explicitly assessed for compliance with any secret-handling policy beyond general hygiene.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were largely purposeful. Password/authentication troubleshooting (cmd-2f9078d3505e4b2d, cmd-88eb415cb1034a98, cmd-0b278e81cfa74b75, cmd-321bc750b0164dcb) involved temporarily setting the replicator role's password to a hardcoded test value ('TestPass123') while diagnosing a scram-sha-256/md5 mismatch; this was a bounded, low-risk diagnostic step that was corrected in the very next command (cmd-51617fed28ec4c11), which restored password_encryption=[REDACTED] as a permanent, necessary fix and reset the replicator password back to the properly generated random value from the .repl_pass file. This chain was a legitimate root-cause fix rather than an abandoned experiment. Temporary replication-password copies placed in /tmp/.repl_pass on node2 and node3 were removed after use (cmd-51bca492e076441b, cmd-a1f4096c32c24291, cmd-099593a806a648c1). One minor residual item: /var/lib/pgsql/.repl_pass (a plaintext copy of the replication password, chmod 600, owned by postgres) remains on node1 at task end -- a low-blast-radius but avoidable secret-on-disk residue. No failed services, damaged package state, or unsafe firewall/network exposure were observed in the after-executor snapshot; port 5432 was opened deliberately and is required for replication traffic.
